source: Du et al. (2023) Guiding Pretraining in Reinforcement Learning with Large Language Models (ELLM)
finding: Founding paper for LLM-suggested goals. An LLM reads a text description of the agent's state and proposes goals. The agent gets a reward when its behaviour matches a goal (sentence-embedding similarity).
numbers: Crafter: ELLM unlocks about 6 achievements per episode in pretraining. Oracle with true rewards: about 9. RND, APT and Novelty: under 3.
limits: Needs a state captioner. Crafter was modified (table needs 1 wood, not 2). Used Codex and Davinci; smaller GPT-3 models gave degraded performance.
agent_relevance: S3 priors: ask the model what is worth trying in this state, instead of rewarding novelty alone.

source: Du et al. (2023) Guiding Pretraining in Reinforcement Learning with Large Language Models (ELLM)
finding: Quality of the LLM goal suggestions was audited. Most were sensible, a minority were not.
numbers: Suggested goals: 64.9% good (achievable, context- and common-sense-sensible), 13.6% violate context sensitivity, 16.4% violate common sense, 5.0% impossible under Crafter physics. Rewarded goals: 66.5% good, 32.4% common-sense violations, 1.1% context violations, 0% impossible.
limits: Rewarded set has more common-sense violations than the suggested set, so the similarity matcher adds noise.
agent_relevance: About one third of model suggestions are not usable. A prior must be checked, not trusted.

source: Du et al. (2023) Guiding Pretraining in Reinforcement Learning with Large Language Models (ELLM)
finding: False negatives from the LLM can permanently block a skill. In Crafter the LLM never suggested making a wood pickaxe.
numbers: Authors suggest mixing ELLM with RND-style novelty to cover this gap.
quote: LLM never suggests creating wood pickaxes
limits: Single case reported by the authors, no frequency given.
agent_relevance: Keep a non-language novelty fallback so one blind spot in the prior cannot close off a branch.

source: Du et al. (2023) Guiding Pretraining in Reinforcement Learning with Large Language Models (ELLM)
finding: Downstream use: a pretrained ELLM policy is used for exploration or finetuning on 7 Crafter tasks and on Housekeep rearrangement.
numbers: Housekeep: LLM yes/no accuracy on object-receptacle fit was above 87% on some measures but only 50-90% on others (Table 3). Crafter: 5 seeds; Figure 8 uses 10 eval trials x 10 episodes x 5 seeds.
limits: Benefit is largest where pretraining already reaches high success; on some tasks gains are small and variance is high.
agent_relevance: Prior helps most when the task lies in the LLM's common knowledge.

source: Du et al. (2023) Guiding Pretraining in Reinforcement Learning with Large Language Models (ELLM)
finding: Prompt wording changed suggestion accuracy but not pretraining success much. A shorter two-example prompt lowered the fraction of good suggestions but kept performance.
numbers: Appendix Table 4 vs main Table 2: suggestion accuracy not perfectly correlated with success.
limits: Only one alternative prompt tested.
agent_relevance: Do not tune the prior prompt only for suggestion precision; measure downstream effect.

source: Du et al. (2023) Guiding Pretraining in Reinforcement Learning with Large Language Models (ELLM)
finding: Learned captioner robustness: ELLM stays fairly robust with an imperfect captioner, but reward confusion is high when achievements share words.
numbers: Captioner trained on 847 human + 900 synthetic labels. False negative rate 11% on average; chop-grass 100% false negative. False positives frequent when achievements share words (wood, stone, collect).
limits: Similarity-based matching of text to behaviour is the weak link.
agent_relevance: When the check that grounds a language idea is fuzzy, expect false credit. Use exact checks (G2, G3).

source: Zhang et al. (2023) OMNI: Open-endedness via Models of human Notions of Interestingness
finding: A foundation model judges which learnable tasks are also interesting. Combined with a learning-progress curriculum, it beats learning progress alone and uniform sampling.
numbers: Crafter (GPT-3 Davinci, few-shot): uniform learns 4 tasks, success 0.030. Learning progress (LP) learns 55 tasks, success 0.42. OMNI (LP + model of interestingness) learns 82 tasks, success 0.56; on interesting tasks only 0.78 vs LP 0.52. Medians with 95% bootstrap CIs; p<1e-3 Mann-Whitney.
limits: LP is distracted by learnable but boring tasks. Gains in BabyAI are small in absolute terms (task success 7.5e-3 OMNI vs 5.9e-3 LP vs 4.7e-3 uniform).
agent_relevance: The model of interestingness is a filter on what to try next, a cheap S3 prior.

source: Zhang et al. (2023) OMNI: Open-endedness via Models of human Notions of Interestingness
finding: The LLM interest filter is almost as good as a hand-built oracle.
numbers: OMNI vs LP + oracle model of interestingness: almost indistinguishable; all but one test p>0.05 across Crafter and BabyAI.
limits: The oracle was defined by the authors, so 'interesting' means their definition (e.g. non-repetitive tasks).
agent_relevance: For a well-defined notion of useful, the LLM prior can be near ceiling.

source: Zhang et al. (2023) OMNI: Open-endedness via Models of human Notions of Interestingness
finding: AI2-THOR with GPT-4 generating new tasks zero-shot from what the agent can and cannot do.
numbers: OMNI learns 13 tasks (CI 11-17) vs LP 2 (CI 0-3) and uniform 0 (CI 0-2); success threshold 0.6.
limits: Small task counts; one embodied domain; the GPT-4 prompt includes lists of successes, so it is partly a feedback loop.
agent_relevance: Model-proposed tasks work when the proposal is conditioned on real success data.

source: Faldor et al. (2024) OMNI-EPIC: Open-endedness via Models of human Notions of Interestingness with Environments Programmed in Code
finding: Extends OMNI: the LLM writes both the task and the environment code, filtered by a model of interestingness, with a task archive.
numbers: In one run RL agents completed 16 tasks, failed 6, and 1 was judged uninteresting. User study: 50 participants, 72.7% agreement between human evaluations and the automatic success detector.
limits: The success detector disagrees with humans on about 27%. Ablations (no archive; learning progress only) were significantly worse on diversity and novelty metrics.
agent_relevance: Self-generated tasks need an external success check; model-judged success is only about 73% aligned with humans.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with Large Language Models
finding: GPT-4 proposes the next task in Minecraft (automatic curriculum) and writes code skills stored in a library.
numbers: 63 unique items in 160 prompting iterations, 3.3x more than baselines. Wooden/stone/iron tool in 6/11/21 iterations (3/3 runs); diamond reached in 1 of 3 runs (102 iterations). AutoGPT 92/94/135 iterations, diamond 0/3. ReAct and Reflexion 0/3 on every level.
limits: Only 3 runs per method. Needs GPT-4 plus text game state; GPT-4 gets 5.7x more unique items than GPT-3.5. Environment feedback is used throughout.
agent_relevance: Directly comparable to our S3: the model proposes what to try next from state and history.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with Large Language Models
finding: Ablation: the curriculum matters a lot, and a hand-made curriculum is worse than the model's.
numbers: Replacing the automatic curriculum with a random one cuts discovered items by 93%. Manual curriculum also falls short. No skill library: plateaus later.
limits: Random curriculum draws from items Voyager itself found, so tasks may be out of order rather than bad.
agent_relevance: Order of what-to-try-next is worth as much as the proposals themselves.

source: Ahn et al. (2022) Do As I Can, Not As I Say (SayCan)
finding: Language model proposals are weighed by a learned affordance value so only feasible actions are chosen.
numbers: 101 instructions, 7 families, PaLM 540B. Mock kitchen: plan success 84%, execution success 74%. Real kitchen: planning drops 3 points, execution drops 14 points.
limits: Needs trained value functions for each skill. Execution success judged by 2 of 3 raters.
agent_relevance: The LLM prior should be gated by a grounded feasibility check, as in G2/G3.

source: Klissarov et al. (2023) Motif: Intrinsic Motivation from Artificial Intelligence Feedback
finding: Llama 2 70B ranks pairs of NetHack message captions; the preferences are distilled into an intrinsic reward.
numbers: Intrinsic reward alone beats an agent trained on the game score on the score task. On sparse tasks Motif + extrinsic reaches about 30% success on the Oracle task; extrinsic-only and RND have 0% on staircase levels 3 and 4.
limits: Authors say it is the first deep-RL agent to beat an extrinsic-reward agent on a dense task using intrinsic reward only. NetHack only.
agent_relevance: Preference over pairs is easier than absolute scoring; fits our compare steps.

source: Klissarov et al. (2023) Motif: Intrinsic Motivation from Artificial Intelligence Feedback
finding: Reward hacking by composition: a good LLM reward combined with the task reward produced a misaligned agent on the Oracle task.
numbers: The agent almost never left level 1 and found a hallucinogen (kill yellow mold, eat corpse) so it hallucinated the oracle, instead of going deep.
limits: Shown on one task; authors name it 'misalignment by composition'.
agent_relevance: Language priors can be gamed. Success must come from the true check, not the proxy.

source: Klissarov et al. (2023) Motif: Intrinsic Motivation from Artificial Intelligence Feedback
finding: Scaling with LLM size and prompt steering.
numbers: Llama 2 7B, 13B, 70B on staircase (level 3): larger LLM gives higher success. Prompt modifiers: +106% gold (CI 64-157%), +17% descents (9-26%), +150% kills (140-161%).
limits: Three sizes of one model family; NetHack metrics only.
agent_relevance: The prior is steerable by wording, and quality grows with model size.

source: Zheng et al. (2025) Online Intrinsic Rewards for Decision Making Agents from Large Language Model Feedback (ONI)
finding: Replicates and extends Motif without its 1-billion-step offline dataset, using an asynchronous LLaMA-3 server and distilled reward models (hash, classification, ranking).
numbers: 5 seeds, 95% CIs. ONI-classification matches Motif on all NetHack tasks except Oracle (still performs well there). Reward-free: ONI-classification beats Motif on 3 of 4 progress metrics. All ONI variants far above extrinsic-only on sparse tasks.
limits: Motif needs an extra 1e9 environment samples from the dense Score task, which is an unrealistic assumption. ELLM-BoW is a strong baseline but cannot tell 'combat' from 'gold' goals.
agent_relevance: Online distillation of LLM judgements is enough; the prior does not need a big offline dataset.

source: Zheng et al. (2025) Online Intrinsic Rewards for Decision Making Agents from Large Language Model Feedback (ONI)
finding: A simple retrieval-based reward does surprisingly well and is often close to the classification reward.
numbers: Figure 3: ONI-retrieval close to ONI-classification on most tasks.
limits: Bag-of-words matching breaks on complex goal strings (Figure 4).
agent_relevance: Cheap lookup of past labelled situations can stand in for repeated LLM calls.

source: Bougie and Watanabe (2025) Exploring Beyond Curiosity Rewards: Language-Driven Exploration in RL (iLLM)
finding: iLLM adds two LLM tasks to curiosity: action generation and history compression (the LLM reads a state-action trajectory description). A Hopfield module maps state-actions to LLM token embeddings so no text description is needed.
numbers: Evaluated on BabyAI-Text (9 tasks), MiniHack, 5 Atari games, Crafter; 10 seeds. Crafter: about 7 achievements per episode vs 6 for the best baseline.
limits: Margin over best baseline on Crafter is 1 achievement; the Atari variant has no text mode.
agent_relevance: The named key work: language as a prior on top of novelty, not instead of it.

source: Bougie and Watanabe (2025) Exploring Beyond Curiosity Rewards: Language-Driven Exploration in RL (iLLM)
finding: Atari results for iLLM(hop), 100M steps, 10 seeds. Authors say RND and NGU score near zero on most tasks and that iLLM beats methods without world knowledge on Montezuma, PrivateEye, Gravitar and Pitfall.
numbers: iLLM(hop): Montezuma 2,632; PrivateEye 4,422; Gravitar 4,044; Pitfall 125; Seaquest 18,851.
limits: Baseline columns in the extracted table were garbled, so baseline numbers are not recorded. Seaquest is not listed among the wins. Authors say gains appear where the LLM has good knowledge.
agent_relevance: The gain follows how much the LLM knows about the domain.

source: Bougie and Watanabe (2025) Exploring Beyond Curiosity Rewards: Language-Driven Exploration in RL (iLLM)
finding: Backbone ablation and noisy-TV test. Larger backbones (Llama-2) help sample efficiency at higher cost; Transformer-XL gave the best trade-off. Translated observations were slightly better than raw text.
numbers: Randomized-TV GoToObj: iLLM(obs) and iLLM(hop) significantly above baselines, paired t-test p<0.002, noise 0.05 and 0.10. Visual noise hurts iLLM(hop) more than iLLM(obs).
limits: Table 4 and 5 values were not recoverable from the PDF text; only the text claims are recorded.
agent_relevance: Language-based novelty is less fooled by random noise than prediction-error novelty.

source: Bougie and Watanabe (2025) Exploring Beyond Curiosity Rewards: Language-Driven Exploration in RL (iLLM)
finding: MiniHack and dense-reward checks. LLM-using methods (ELLM, PAE, iLLM) beat pure curiosity (RND, NGU). ELLM's score is capped by LLM mistakes in MiniHack. In dense BabyAI tasks the authors test that iLLM does not hurt.
numbers: Table 2 and Table 7 values not extracted; Table 6 measures distance to human demonstrations.
limits: Authors' own comparisons; Pangu, ChibiT, PAE results taken from other papers where available.
agent_relevance: Check the prior does not hurt when reward is already dense.

source: Carta et al. (2023) Grounding Large Language Models in Interactive Environments with Online RL (GLAM)
finding: Counter-approach: use the LLM as the policy and finetune it with PPO. LLM knowledge speeds learning, but needs grounding.
numbers: BabyAI-Text, 4 seeds, 1.5M steps: GFlan-T5 reaches 0.8 success after 250k steps and 0.9 after about 600k. DRRN and NPAE-Flan-T5 still below 0.2 at 1.5M. Symbolic-PPO about 0.4. With 4 to 16 distractors GFlan-T5 drops 14% vs 38% for the comparison agent.
limits: Small environment, Flan-T5 finetuned; all agents fail on new tasks (Q3); success drops 13% with invented objects.
agent_relevance: A training-free scaffold cannot do this; it marks the limit of pure prompting.

source: Krishnamurthy et al. (2024) Can Large Language Models Explore In-Context?
finding: Native LLM exploration is poor. In bandits, only one configuration explored well: GPT-4 + hint to explore + externally summarised per-arm averages + zero-shot chain of thought.
numbers: Main setting K=5 arms, gap 0.2, T=100. Gpt-3.5: 48 configs x N=20 replicates; Gpt-4: 72 configs; Llama2 also tested. Basic GPT-4 prompt: suffix failure (never picks the best arm again) in more than 60% of replicates. Baselines 1000 replicates.
quote: fails to select the best arm even once after some initial rounds
limits: Simple bandits only. The same prompt without external summary fails. Authors warn that a summary may be hard to build in complex tasks.
agent_relevance: Strong support for code-computed summaries and counts feeding S3, not model-held history.

source: Krishnamurthy et al. (2024) Can Large Language Models Explore In-Context?
finding: Second failure mode: the model behaves almost uniformly, picking all arms about equally and never narrowing down.
numbers: Observed across several Gpt-3.5 and Llama2 configurations.
limits: Descriptive; per-configuration counts are in the appendix.
agent_relevance: The model's own proposals cannot be relied on for explore/exploit balance; the program should own that.

source: Quadros et al. (2025) LLM-Driven Intrinsic Motivation for Sparse Reward Reinforcement Learning
finding: Small test in MiniGrid DoorKey 8x8 with A2C: LLM reward plus variational novelty. Results were mixed across configurations.
numbers: 3 runs per config. Plain A2C failed to learn. VAE-only config reached mean reward above 0.6; LLM+VAE 1 stayed below 0.2 after 5000 episodes; LLM+VAE 2 and 3 did well. Considerable run-to-run variation.
limits: Tiny study, 3 runs, hyperparameter sensitive; the authors say exploration failures need tuning. The combined benefit is fragile.
agent_relevance: The LLM bonus is not reliably additive; test before relying on it.

source: Ma et al. (2023) Eureka: Human-Level Reward Design via Coding Large Language Models
finding: GPT-4 writes reward code, evolutionary search runs over candidates, and reward reflection (a text summary of training statistics) improves it.
numbers: 29 environments, 10 robot morphologies. Beats expert human rewards on 83% of tasks. Average normalised improvement 52%.
limits: Needs a simulator with fast reward evaluation. Reward reflection depends on real training output.
agent_relevance: Supports revision from real measured output (G2).

source: Pattern across the above (our synthesis)
finding: Language priors help where the LLM already knows the domain (Crafter, NetHack), help little or hurt where it errs (MiniHack for ELLM, missing pickaxe), and need a grounded check against reward hacking (Motif Oracle task). Independent replication is thin: ONI is the main one, Quadros is mixed.
numbers: Six papers report gains in common-knowledge domains; two give explicit failure cases; one small study is mixed.
limits: Mostly one research cluster and mostly game domains.
agent_relevance: S3 priors should be a proposal list that code can verify, with a novelty or random fallback.
